title: How to Not Get Drunk: Pacing Tips That Actually Work
excerpt: How to drink without getting drunk: why only pace and amount really matter, the one-drink-an-hour rule, spacers, the water myth, food, mixers, and social tactics.
metaDescription: How to not get drunk: pace yourself at one drink an hour, use spacers, eat first, avoid diet mixers, and skip the myths that do not work.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the only thing that reliably keeps you from getting drunk is drinking alcohol more slowly than your body can clear it. Your liver works through roughly one standard drink per hour, and nothing you eat, drink, or swallow makes it go meaningfully faster. So the practical playbook is about pace and amount: eat a real meal before you start, aim for about one drink an hour, put a glass of water or a soft drink between every alcoholic one, pick lower-strength drinks, and decide your limit before you walk in the door. Most "tricks" you'll hear, from shots of olive oil to chugging coffee, either don't work or make things worse.

**The quick rules:** Eat a proper meal with protein and fat before drinking. Know what a standard drink actually is, because most pours are bigger. Sip, don't gulp, and alternate every drink with a non-alcoholic one. Avoid shots, drinking games, and fizzy or diet mixers that speed up absorption. Keep your own glass in your hand so nobody tops it up. And remember that once you feel drunk, there is no way to "sober up" quickly. Only time lowers your blood alcohol.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide is about moderating your drinking at social events. It does not make any amount of alcohol safe for driving, and it isn't a plan for people who are pregnant, under 21, taking medicines that interact with alcohol, or advised by a doctor not to drink. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if someone** is confused or can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, has slow or irregular breathing (fewer than about eight breaths a minute or long gaps between breaths), has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning. Don't let them "sleep it off." Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) covers what to do while you wait for help.

## Why You Get Drunk: The One Number That Matters

"Drunk" is your brain reacting to the amount of alcohol in your blood, measured as blood alcohol concentration (BAC). If you want a plain-words explainer of the number itself, see [what BAC means](/never-hungover/what-is-bac). The key idea for staying in control is simple: your BAC goes up when alcohol enters your bloodstream faster than your liver can remove it.

The removal side is fixed. Your liver breaks down alcohol at a fairly steady rate, often quoted as about one standard drink per hour for an average adult, although it varies from person to person. You can't train it, sweat it out, or speed it up in any useful way in one evening. Our article on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism) goes into why.

That leaves the intake side, and you control almost all of it:

- **How much alcohol** you drink in total.
- **How fast** you drink it.
- **How fast it's absorbed** from your stomach and gut into your blood, which depends on food, the type of drink, and what it's mixed with.

Every useful tip in this guide works on one of those three levers. If a tip doesn't change how much, how fast, or how quickly it's absorbed, it probably doesn't work.

### What counts as one drink

In the US, the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) defines a standard drink as about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly:

| Drink | Standard size | Typical alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Regular beer | 12 oz | about 5% |
| Wine | 5 oz | about 12% |
| Distilled spirits (vodka, whiskey, rum, tequila) | 1.5 oz (one shot) | about 40% |
| Malt liquor | 8 to 9 oz | about 7% |

The trap is that real-world servings are often bigger than these. A craft IPA at 7 to 9% in a 16 oz pint can equal two standard drinks or more. A generous restaurant wine pour can be closer to 1.5 or 2 drinks. A cocktail like a Long Island iced tea or a strong margarita may contain two or three shots. If you count "drinks" by the glass rather than by the alcohol in it, you can be off by half or more without realizing. Our guide on [how many drinks it takes to get drunk](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-to-get-drunk) shows how fast these add up for different body sizes.

## How to Pace Yourself: The One-Drink-an-Hour Rule

Pacing is the most effective thing you can do, and it's the part people skip. The goal is to keep your intake close to what your body can process. In practice:

1. **Aim for about one standard drink per hour.** This won't keep your BAC at zero, because absorption and clearance don't line up perfectly, but it keeps it rising slowly instead of spiking.
2. **Make the first drink last.** The first hour is where most people over-drink, because they arrive thirsty, nervous, or hungry. Drink water or a soft drink first to deal with thirst, then start the alcohol.
3. **Sip, don't gulp.** Put the glass down between sips. People drinking from a glass they hold the whole time tend to finish it faster.
4. **Watch the clock, not the crowd.** You don't have to match anyone's pace. If you notice you're halfway through your drink after fifteen minutes, slow down.
5. **Set a number in advance.** Deciding "three drinks tonight" before you arrive works much better than deciding in the moment, because alcohol itself weakens the part of your judgment that would stop you.
6. **Stop earlier than you think you need to.** Alcohol keeps being absorbed for a while after your last sip, so your BAC can keep climbing for 30 to 90 minutes after you put the glass down. The drink you have when you "feel fine" can be the one that tips you over later.

A simple way to keep count is to move a coin or a hair tie from one pocket to the other with each drink, or to note each one in your phone. It sounds silly, but after the third drink almost nobody remembers accurately.

## Use Spacers: Alternate Every Drink

A "spacer" is any non-alcoholic drink you have between alcoholic ones: water, sparkling water, soda, a mocktail, or a non-alcoholic beer. It's one of the easiest habits to adopt, and it works for a plain reason. If you alternate, you're holding a drink the whole night but only half of them contain alcohol. That roughly halves your intake over the same number of hours without making you feel like you're sitting out.

Some tips for making spacers stick:

- **Order them in the same glass.** Soda water with lime in a rocks glass looks exactly like a vodka soda. Nobody asks questions.
- **Use non-alcoholic beer or alcohol-free spirits.** These have gotten much better, and they give you the taste and the ritual without the alcohol. Check the label, as some "non-alcoholic" beers can contain up to 0.5% alcohol.
- **Make the spacer the default.** "Water, then a drink" as a fixed rule is easier than deciding each time.

## The Water Myth: What Water Does and Doesn't Do

You'll often hear that drinking water "dilutes" alcohol or keeps you sober. That's a myth. Water doesn't lower the amount of alcohol in your blood, and it doesn't speed up how quickly your liver breaks it down. Two drinks with six glasses of water will raise your BAC about as much as two drinks with none.

Water still helps, just for different reasons:

- **It slows your pace.** Every minute spent drinking water is a minute you're not drinking alcohol. This is the real benefit, and it's a big one.
- **It deals with thirst.** People often drink beer or cocktails fast because they're thirsty. Quenching thirst with water first stops you treating alcohol like a thirst-quencher.
- **It helps with how you feel.** Alcohol makes you pee more, and some of the next-day headache and dry mouth comes from that fluid loss. Water helps with that part, though it won't prevent a hangover on its own. Our piece on [whether water helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover) covers the details.

So drink water, but understand why. It's a pacing tool, not an antidote.

## Eat a Real Meal Before (and While) You Drink

Food in your stomach is the most powerful thing you can do to slow absorption. When your stomach is empty, alcohol moves quickly into the small intestine, where most of it is absorbed fast. When there's food in your stomach, the valve at the bottom of the stomach stays closed longer while the food is digested, so alcohol trickles through more slowly. This is well established in research on drinking with and without food: the same amount of alcohol produces a lower and later peak BAC after a meal.

What helps most:

- **A full meal, not a snack.** A real dinner does far more than a handful of chips.
- **Protein, fat, and fiber.** These take longer to digest, so they keep your stomach busy longer. Think chicken, fish, eggs, beans, rice, pasta, vegetables, or a burger.
- **Keep eating through the night.** Snacking while you drink helps keep absorption slower.

What doesn't help: a slice of bread doesn't "soak up" alcohol like a sponge. Food helps by slowing your stomach down, not by absorbing the alcohol. And food only slows absorption. It doesn't make the alcohol disappear, so you'll still absorb all of it eventually. For more, see our guides on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) and [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide).

## Choose Your Drinks Wisely

The drink you pick changes how much alcohol you get per sip and how fast it's absorbed.

### Pick lower-strength drinks

A light beer at around 4% gives you a lot more drinking time per gram of alcohol than a double IPA at 9%. Wine spritzers (wine topped with soda water), shandies (beer mixed with lemonade), and session beers all let you hold a drink for longer while taking in less alcohol. Check the ABV on the can or menu, because it varies a lot within the same type of drink.

### Skip shots and drinking games

Shots put a full standard drink into your stomach in two seconds. Drinking games are designed to make you drink faster than you would otherwise. Both are the quickest routes from "fine" to "too drunk," because they push a lot of alcohol in before you can feel the effect of the first round. If you want to join in, take a token sip, or swap your shot for water.

### Be careful with fizzy and diet mixers

Two things about mixers can raise your BAC more than you'd expect:

- **Carbonation.** Some studies have found that alcohol mixed with a carbonated mixer is absorbed faster than the same alcohol mixed with flat water, though results vary between people and not everyone shows the effect. This is one reason champagne and vodka sodas can feel like they hit quickly.
- **Diet mixers.** A study by Cecile Marczinski and Amy Stamates, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2013, found that vodka mixed with a diet soda produced a higher breath alcohol level than the same vodka with a regular, sugar-sweetened soda. The likely reason is that sugar slows how fast the stomach empties, while artificial sweeteners don't.

That doesn't mean you have to drink sugary cocktails, but if you're choosing between a vodka with diet soda and a vodka with juice, the second will usually be absorbed a bit more slowly.

### Watch out for "hidden" alcohol

Cocktails, punches, jungle juice, and sangria make it very hard to know what you're drinking. A sweet punch can hide a lot of spirits, and refills from a shared bowl are impossible to count. When you can't tell what's in a drink, count it as at least two.

### Be careful mixing alcohol and energy drinks

Caffeine doesn't lower your BAC, but it can make you feel more alert than you really are, which can lead people to keep drinking past the point where they'd usually stop. Our guide to [energy drinks and alcohol](/never-hungover/energy-drinks-and-alcohol) explains the "wide-awake drunk" effect.

## Why Some People Get Drunk Faster

Two people drinking the same thing at the same pace can end up at very different BACs. The main reasons:

- **Body size and body water.** Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. A smaller person has less water to dilute it in, so the same drink produces a higher BAC.
- **Sex.** On average, women have a lower proportion of body water than men of the same weight, and research suggests they may break down less alcohol in the stomach before it reaches the blood. The result is that women often reach a higher BAC from the same amount.
- **Food.** As above, an empty stomach can make the same drink hit much harder.
- **Medications.** Many common medicines, including antihistamines, sleep aids, some antidepressants, anti-anxiety drugs, and opioid painkillers, add to alcohol's sedating effect. Check the label or ask a pharmacist before drinking on any medication.
- **Fatigue and illness.** Being tired, sick, or dehydrated can make you feel the effects more strongly, even if your BAC is the same.
- **Tolerance.** People who drink often may feel less drunk at a given BAC. That's a trap, not a strength: their BAC and their reaction time are just as affected even if they feel fine.

## Social Tactics: How to Drink Less Without Making It a Thing

A lot of over-drinking comes from social pressure rather than wanting another drink. These tactics help you stay in control without explaining yourself:

- **Keep a drink in your hand.** People rarely offer you a drink if you're already holding one. A soda water with lime works perfectly.
- **Avoid rounds.** Buying rounds in a group means you drink at the pace of the fastest drinker. Offer to get your own, or skip a round with "I'm still working on this one."
- **Don't let people top you up.** At dinners and parties, refills make it impossible to count. Finish your glass before accepting more, or put your hand over it.
- **Have a short, boring reason ready.** "I'm driving," "early start tomorrow," or "I'm taking it easy tonight" ends most conversations. You don't owe anyone more than that.
- **Be the one with a job.** Hosting, grilling, DJing, or being the photographer gives you something to do with your hands that isn't drinking.
- **Plan your exit.** Decide when you're leaving. The last hour of a long night is when most people drink the most and enjoy it the least.
- **Drink with people who pace like you.** If your friends always go hard, it helps to have one person who's on the same plan as you.

## Situations Where Pacing Matters Most

### Work events and networking

At a work happy hour or holiday party, the goal is to stay sharp. One or two drinks across the whole event, a full meal beforehand, and soda water in between is a solid plan. Hold your drink in your non-dominant hand so you're ready to shake hands, and stop well before the end.

### Weddings and long celebrations

Weddings combine an empty stomach during the ceremony, free drinks, champagne toasts, and an event that lasts six or more hours. Eat before you go, have water during the cocktail hour, sip the toast instead of draining it, and remember that a long day of slow drinking still adds up.

### Dates

Nerves make people drink faster. Order something you'll sip slowly, eat with your drinks, and alternate with water. You'll remember the conversation, which is the point.

### Vacations and day drinking

Sun, heat, and drinking from noon are a rough combination. You lose more fluid in the heat, and a long day makes it easy to lose count. Start later, eat lunch, use lower-strength drinks, and keep water with you.

## Myths That Won't Keep You Sober

These are popular, but there is no good evidence that any of them prevent you from getting drunk:

- **"Line your stomach with olive oil or milk."** A spoonful of oil or a glass of milk is far less effective than a real meal. Eating properly is what works.
- **"Coffee sobers you up."** Caffeine can make you feel more awake, but it doesn't lower your BAC or improve your judgment and coordination. You're just a more alert drunk person.
- **"A cold shower or fresh air will fix it."** These can make you feel more awake for a few minutes. Your BAC doesn't change.
- **"Throwing up gets the alcohol out."** Once alcohol has been absorbed, vomiting doesn't remove it. Vomiting while very drunk is dangerous because of the risk of choking.
- **"Beer before liquor, never been sicker."** The order of drinks matters much less than the total amount and the pace. People who switch to liquor later in the night are often drinking faster by then.
- **"Pills can keep you sober."** No supplement or medicine available over the counter makes you stay sober while drinking normally. More on DHM below.
- **"I'm fine, I've only had a few."** Feeling fine is not a reliable sign of a safe BAC, especially for regular drinkers. And BAC can keep rising after your last drink.

For the full picture on getting alcohol out of your system, see [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up).

## If You've Already Had Too Much

If you notice you've gone past your limit, stop drinking alcohol now. Switch to water, eat something if you can, and sit down somewhere safe. Let a friend know how you're feeling and don't go off alone. Arrange a ride home with a sober driver, a taxi, or a rideshare. Never drive, ride a bike, or swim after drinking.

Remember that your BAC may keep climbing for a while after your last drink. If you start to feel worse instead of better, or you're with someone who does, keep an eye on the warning signs below.

> **When to get help right away.** Call 911 if someone who has been drinking is confused or unresponsive, can't be woken, is vomiting while not fully awake, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has pale, bluish, or cold and clammy skin. Turn them on their side so they don't choke if they vomit, stay with them, and don't give them coffee, a cold shower, or more food or drink to "sober them up." In the US, Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) can also give advice. It's always better to call and not need it than the other way around. Our guide on [being blackout drunk](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains why memory loss is also a warning sign that you drank too much too fast.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, and you'll see it marketed in hangover supplements. It's worth being clear about what it can and can't do.

A well-known 2012 study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* by Shen and colleagues found that DHM reduced signs of intoxication in rats and appeared to block some of alcohol's effects on brain receptors. That research is interesting, but it was in animals, and there is no good evidence that DHM lowers your BAC, keeps you sober, or makes it safe to drink more or drive. Alcohol still affects your judgment and coordination whether or not you take any supplement.

Where some people find it useful is for the morning after: DHM is studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, and many people take it before bed after a night of moderate drinking hoping to feel better the next day. The evidence in people is still limited, so treat it as a possible extra, not a replacement for pacing, food, and water. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. For the broader set of habits that make the next day easier, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

You can't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol, so the only way not to get drunk is to control how much you drink and how fast it reaches your blood. Eat a real meal first, know what a standard drink looks like, aim for about one an hour, alternate every drink with water or a soft drink, avoid shots and diet or fizzy mixers, and decide your limit before you start. Water, coffee, and supplements won't sober you up, and once you're drunk, only time helps. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, call for help right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How can I drink without getting drunk?**

Eat a full meal first, aim for about one standard drink per hour, alternate every alcoholic drink with water or a soft drink, choose lower-strength drinks, and avoid shots and drinking games. Set a limit before you start. Your liver clears alcohol at a roughly fixed rate, so controlling how much and how fast you drink is the only approach that reliably works.

**How do you pace yourself when drinking?**

Start with a glass of water so you're not thirsty, then sip your first drink slowly and make it last about an hour. Put your glass down between sips, alternate each alcoholic drink with a non-alcoholic one, skip rounds so you're not matching the fastest drinker, and keep count with your phone or a coin in your pocket. Stop before you feel drunk, because your BAC can keep rising after your last drink.

**Does drinking water stop you from getting drunk?**

No. Water doesn't dilute the alcohol in your blood or speed up how fast your liver clears it. It helps by slowing your pace, since time spent drinking water is time not spent drinking alcohol, and by replacing some of the fluid alcohol makes you lose. Use it as a pacing tool, not an antidote.

**What should I eat so I don't get drunk fast?**

A full meal with protein, fat, and fiber, such as chicken, fish, eggs, rice, pasta, beans, or a burger, eaten before you start and topped up with snacks during the night. Food keeps alcohol in your stomach longer so it's absorbed more slowly and your peak BAC is lower. Food slows absorption but doesn't stop it, so you still need to pace yourself.

**Can coffee or a cold shower sober you up?**

No. Caffeine and cold water can make you feel more awake, but they don't lower your blood alcohol or restore your judgment and coordination. Only time does that. Being awake but still drunk can actually be riskier, because people may think they're fine to drive or keep drinking.

**Which drinks get you drunk fastest?**

Shots and strong cocktails, because they deliver a lot of alcohol quickly. Studies also suggest that carbonated mixers and diet (sugar-free) mixers can make alcohol absorb faster than flat or sugar-sweetened mixers. Lower-strength options like light beer, wine spritzers, and shandies let you drink for longer while taking in less alcohol.

**Does DHM keep you from getting drunk?**

There is no good evidence that DHM keeps you sober or lowers your BAC in people. An early study found it reduced signs of intoxication in rats, but that hasn't been shown in humans. Alcohol still affects your judgment and coordination whether or not you take it, so never use any supplement as a reason to drink more or to drive.

**How do I say no to drinks without making it awkward?**

Keep a non-alcoholic drink in your hand, since people rarely offer a drink to someone already holding one. Have a short reason ready, such as driving or an early start, and skip rounds by saying you're still working on your drink. You don't owe anyone a longer explanation.
